lead: Feedback lets you swap raw gain for a gain you can trust, a wider bandwidth and impedances you choose. Push the same loop past unity and the amplifier sings: that is where sine-wave oscillators come from. After this unit you can compute closed-loop gain and impedance, read gain and phase margins off a Bode plot, and design an RC, LC or crystal oscillator for a given frequency.
about: The unit follows one loop around an amplifier. Chapter 4.1 places a feedback factor β beside the gain A and shows what the factor 1+Aβ does to gain, bandwidth and distortion. Chapter 4.2 splits feedback into four kinds, because only the mixing and sampling decide whether an impedance rises or falls. Chapter 4.3 treats the loop gain as a complex number and reads stability from Bode plots. Chapter 4.4 keeps the loop but makes the feedback positive and states the Barkhausen condition. Chapters 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7 use that condition to build real oscillators: RC networks, LC tanks and quartz crystals, each trading frequency stability against cost, size and tuning range.

chapters.idea: Returning a fraction β of the output to the input in opposition cuts the gain by 1+Aβ and spends that cut on a wider bandwidth, lower distortion and a gain fixed by β alone.
chapters.depth: Block diagram with A (open-loop gain, V/V) and β (feedback factor, V/V). Summing node, v_f = βv_o, v_i = v_s − v_f. Closed-loop gain A_f = A/(1+Aβ). Loop gain = Aβ. Desensitivity D = 1+Aβ. When Aβ is much greater than 1, A_f ≈ 1/β and the gain stops depending on the transistor. Gain spread, harmonic distortion and the feedback-corrected part of noise all shrink by D. Bandwidth stretches by D, so A_f × BW equals the open-loop gain-bandwidth product. Say clearly that β alone does not decide whether an impedance rises or falls (that is 4.2), and that the poles move as β changes (that is 4.3). Numbers only, no pole algebra.

figure.title: Negative feedback loop
figure.aria: Blocks showing the source, summing node, amplifier A and output, with the β network returning βv_o to the summing node.

chapters.example: An amplifier has A = 1000 V/V, bandwidth 10 kHz and β = 0.01. Find the loop gain, the closed-loop gain, the new bandwidth, and the change in closed-loop gain when A rises by 10 %. Answer: Aβ = 1000 × 0.01 = 10, D = 1 + 10 = 11, A_f = 1000/11 = 90.9 V/V, bandwidth = 10 kHz × 11 = 110 kHz, and ΔA_f/A_f = 10 %/11 = 0.91 %.
chapters.trap: Writing A_f = A/(1 − Aβ), or jumping to A_f ≈ 1/β when Aβ is only 3 or 4. Check the size of Aβ before you approximate.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (common-emitter gain, loading) and Unit 3 (gain-bandwidth product, cut-off frequency).
chapters.leave: Which impedance moves and in which direction goes to 4.2. The movement of poles and the arrival of instability goes to 4.3.

chapters.idea: Four topologies come from two independent choices — sample the output voltage or the output current, and mix the returning signal in series or in shunt at the input — and each choice fixes one impedance.
chapters.depth: Define sampling: voltage sampling connects the feedback network across the output node; current sampling puts it in series with the output loop. Define mixing: series mixing subtracts a feedback voltage in the input loop; shunt mixing subtracts a feedback current at the input node. Give all four with both naming styles: voltage-series (series-shunt), voltage-shunt (shunt-shunt), current-series (series-series), current-shunt (shunt-series). Table of effects: input resistance rises for series mixing and falls for shunt mixing; output resistance falls for voltage sampling and rises for current sampling. Give the ideal closed-loop gain of each with its unit: V/V, A/V (transconductance), V/A (transresistance), A/A. Mention loading by the feedback network in one or two lines. Keep identification practical: look at the output node, then at the input node.

figure.aria: Tree of four feedback topologies branching from voltage or current sampling, each into series or shunt mixing.

chapters.example: A voltage-series feedback amplifier has A = 10⁴ V/V, β = 0.01 V/V, input resistance 10 kΩ and output resistance 1 kΩ. Find D, A_f, the input resistance and the output resistance with feedback. Answer: D = 1 + 10⁴ × 0.01 = 101, A_f = 10⁴/101 = 99.0 V/V, R_if = 10 kΩ × 101 = 1.01 MΩ, R_of = 1 kΩ/101 = 9.9 Ω.
chapters.trap: Quoting 'negative feedback raises input impedance' as a general rule. Only series mixing raises input resistance, and only voltage sampling lowers output resistance.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for A, β and D; Unit 2 for amplifier input and output resistance.
chapters.leave: Op-amp versions of these four topologies go to Unit 6. The general return-ratio and stability treatment goes to 4.3.

chapters.idea: The loop gain Aβ is a complex function of frequency, and the amplifier stays stable as long as its magnitude falls below 1 before the loop phase reaches −180°.
chapters.depth: Loop gain T(jω) = A(jω)β(jω) with magnitude and phase. Characteristic equation 1 + T(s) = 0; the closed-loop poles are its roots, and as β rises the poles move toward the right half plane (show the picture, no root-locus construction). Bode magnitude plot in dB with 20 dB/decade per pole; phase plot with −45° at each pole and −90° per pole well above it. Gain crossover frequency (|T| = 1, that is 0 dB) and phase crossover frequency (phase = −180°). Phase margin = 180° + ∠T at the gain crossover. Gain margin = −20 log|T| in dB at the phase crossover, positive when stable. Design target 45° to 60° of phase margin. A one-pole loop is always stable, two poles can be made safe, three poles easily ring. State plainly that adding feedback moves the amplifier poles, which is why the open-loop Bode plot answers a closed-loop question.

figure.aria: Plot of the loop gain falling at 20 dB per decade and crossing the 0 dB line at 10 kHz.

chapters.example: An amplifier has open-loop gain A₀ = 10⁵, poles at 10 Hz and 100 kHz, and β = 0.01. Find the low-frequency loop gain, the gain crossover frequency, the phase margin and the gain margin. Answer: |Aβ| at low frequency = 10⁵ × 0.01 = 1000, that is 60 dB. Above 10 Hz the gain falls as 10⁶/f, so |A| = 100 (|Aβ| = 1) at f = 10 kHz. Phase there = −90° (from the 10 Hz pole) − arctan(10⁴/10⁵) = −90° − 5.7° = −95.7°, so phase margin = 180° − 95.7° = 84.3°. The phase never reaches −180°, so the gain margin is infinite on paper.
chapters.trap: Measuring the gain margin at the gain crossover and the phase margin at the phase crossover. Each margin belongs to the other crossing, and the sign convention makes a stable amplifier report a positive gain margin.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 and 4.2 for β and loop gain; Unit 3 for Bode plots, poles and cut-off frequencies.
chapters.leave: Compensation networks and op-amp internal compensation go to Unit 5. Making the loop oscillate on purpose goes to 4.4.

chapters.idea: An oscillator is a feedback amplifier with positive feedback whose loop gain equals exactly one at one frequency — magnitude 1 and total loop phase a whole multiple of 360°.
chapters.depth: Positive feedback: the returned signal adds to the input. Barkhausen condition: |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0° (some syllabi write 360°) at the oscillation frequency f₀. The phase condition picks f₀; the magnitude condition gives the minimum amplifier gain. Start-up needs |Aβ| slightly greater than 1 so noise and switching transients grow; amplitude limiting then pulls the loop back to 1 through transistor cut-off and saturation, bias shift, diode limiters or a thermistor. No external input is needed, only the DC supply. Classify oscillators: RC (audio, poor stability), LC (radio frequency), crystal (best stability). Add the honest caveat: Barkhausen is necessary but not sufficient for a clean sine wave, because amplitude control and a reasonably linear amplifier decide the distortion.

figure.title: Oscillator loop
figure.aria: Loop of summing node, amplifier and output with the β network feeding back in phase so that the loop gain is one at the oscillation frequency.

chapters.example: An inverting amplifier has gain A = −50 and drives a feedback network that shifts the phase by a further 180° at 5 kHz with β = 0.02. Check Barkhausen. Answer: Aβ = −50 × 0.02 = −1, so |Aβ| = 1, and the total loop phase is 180° + 180° = 360°. The circuit oscillates at 5 kHz. If β is raised to 0.03, |Aβ| = 1.5: the amplitude grows until the amplifier clips and the average loop gain settles back to 1.
chapters.trap: Checking only the magnitude. Both conditions are needed, and the 180° inversion of the amplifier counts as part of the loop phase.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for β and loop gain, 4.3 for loop phase.
chapters.leave: Circuit realisations go to 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7. Astable, monostable and bistable multivibrators and the 555 timer go to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: An RC network gives a frequency-dependent phase shift, so three sections — or one lead-lag section — select the single frequency at which the loop satisfies Barkhausen.
chapters.depth: RC phase-shift oscillator: three identical RC sections, about 60° each at f₀, giving 180°, with an inverting amplifier supplying the other 180°. f₀ = 1/(2πRC√6); the network passes only 1/29 of the signal at f₀, so the amplifier needs a gain of at least 29 (a BJT stage with hfe above 29 plus bias, or an op-amp). Wien bridge: a series RC and a parallel RC form a lead-lag network across the amplifier; f₀ = 1/(2πRC), the feedback fraction is exactly 1/3 at f₀, so the amplifier gain must be 3 (non-inverting op-amp with 1 + R_f/R_i = 3). Amplitude stabilisation with a small lamp, thermistor or diode limiter, because the gain must start just above the threshold. Compare the two: Wien has one frequency-setting pair, lower distortion and easier tuning; the RC phase-shift circuit is simpler but needs high gain and drifts more. Numeric design of R and C for a target frequency.

figure.aria: Plot of the Wien network feedback fraction rising to one third at ωRC equal to one and falling on both sides.

chapters.example: Design an RC phase-shift oscillator for 1 kHz using C = 10 nF in each section. Find R and the minimum amplifier gain, then use the same R and C in a Wien bridge. Answer: R = 1/(2π f C √6) = 1/(15.39 × 1000 × 10⁻⁸) = 6.5 kΩ, and the amplifier gain must be at least 29 with 180° inversion. In a Wien bridge with the same 6.5 kΩ and 10 nF, f = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 6500 × 10⁻⁸) = 2449 Hz, and the amplifier gain must be exactly 3.
chapters.trap: Swapping the constants. The √6 and the gain 29 belong to the three-section RC phase-shift oscillator; the Wien bridge has no √6 and needs a gain of 3.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for Barkhausen; Unit 3 for RC frequency response; Unit 2 for the inverting amplifier.
chapters.leave: LC and crystal oscillators go to 4.6 and 4.7. Op-amp gain equations go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An LC tank shows a high impedance only near its resonant frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(L_eq C_eq)), and a tap on the inductor or the capacitor returns just enough output to keep the circuit oscillating there.
chapters.depth: Parallel tank: resonance, Q = R/ω₀L = ω₀CR, impedance peak R at f₀, zero phase at f₀ and about ±90° away from it. Hartley: tap between two series inductors, L_eq = L1 + L2 (add 2M if they are coupled), f₀ = 1/(2π√(L_eq C)), feedback fraction set by the coil ratio. Colpitts: tapped capacitors, C_eq = C1C2/(C1+C2), f₀ = 1/(2π√(L C_eq)), preferred at high frequency because the capacitive divider swamps transistor capacitances. Clapp: a Colpitts with a small C3 in series with L, so C_eq is nearly C3 and the frequency hardly depends on the transistor; narrower tuning range, higher Q. In every case the amplifier gain must be at least the inverse of the divider fraction. Keep Q's effect on selectivity qualitative, and note that these circuits are the tuned oscillators behind radio transmitters. Skip full h-parameter derivations.

figure.aria: Plot of tank impedance against frequency, peaking at f₀ and much sharper for the higher Q.

chapters.example: A Hartley oscillator uses L1 = 100 µH, L2 = 10 µH (no mutual inductance) and C = 200 pF. Find the frequency and the minimum amplifier gain. Answer: L_eq = 100 + 10 = 110 µH, f₀ = 1/(2π√(110 × 10⁻⁶ × 200 × 10⁻¹²)) = 1/(2π × 1.483 × 10⁻⁷) = 1.07 MHz. The tap returns L2/(L1+L2) = 10/110 = 0.091 of the output, so the amplifier needs a gain of at least 11. Using L1 alone would wrongly give 1.13 MHz.
chapters.trap: Putting one coil into the frequency formula. In a Hartley oscillator the frequency depends on L1 + L2, not on L1 or L2 alone, and the gain must still exceed the inverse of the tap fraction.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for Barkhausen; Unit 2 for BJT gain; Unit 3 for tuned amplifiers and Q.
chapters.leave: Crystal resonators go to 4.7. The phase-locked loop and voltage-controlled oscillator go to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: A quartz crystal is a piezoelectric resonator with Q in the tens of thousands, so an oscillator built around it holds its frequency to a few parts per million.
chapters.depth: Piezoelectric effect: a quartz slice between two plates behaves as a very high-Q series LCR branch in parallel with C₀, the electrode capacitance. Two resonances: series resonance f_s = 1/(2π√(LC)), where the crystal looks like a small resistance; parallel resonance f_p = f_s√(1 + C/C₀), where it behaves as an inductor. The two lie a fraction of a percent apart. Circuits: the crystal in the feedback path working in series-resonant mode, or as the inductor of a Colpitts or Pierce circuit in parallel mode. Typical values: 32.768 kHz for watches and real-time clocks, 1 MHz to 30 MHz for microcontrollers and radios, tolerance 10 to 100 ppm plus temperature drift, and trim capacitors that pull the frequency slightly. Compare with an LC tank: far higher Q, no coil, far better stability, but a fixed frequency and a fragile part. One line on overtone operation if space allows.

figure.aria: Stack of oscillator types from RC networks down to atomic clocks, each more stable than the one above.

chapters.example: A 1 MHz crystal has series resistance 100 Ω and Q = 10⁵, with C₀ = 3 pF. Find L, C and the parallel resonant frequency. Answer: L = QR/ω = (10⁵ × 100)/(2π × 10⁶) = 1.59 H. Then C = 1/(ω²L) = 1/((2π × 10⁶)² × 1.59) = 0.016 pF. f_p = f_s√(1 + C/C₀) = 1 MHz × √(1 + 0.016/3) = 1.00265 MHz, only 2.65 kHz above the series resonance.
chapters.trap: Assuming a crystal has a single resonant frequency. Series and parallel resonance differ, and C₀ must be included whenever f_p is asked.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for Barkhausen and 4.6 for the LC tank and Q.
chapters.leave: PLL frequency synthesis, clock dividers and the 555 timer go to Unit 7.
